newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: INSOLVENCY ON RISE IN YUGOSLAVIA - ECONOMISTS.
newsitem.headline: INSOLVENCY ON RISE IN YUGOSLAVIA - ECONOMISTS.

text.p: The number of insolvent firms in Yugoslavia rose further in December despite relaxed monetary policy and are a big burden on the country's cash-strapped economy, economists said on Thursday.

"An enormous number of permanently insolvent firms and their unpaid liabilities additionally burden the already exhausted economy," Slobodan Milisavljevic of the Belgrade-based Market Research Institute (IZIT) told Reuters.
"They make it difficult to maintain the production process, and have particularly negative effects on efforts to boost output and exports," he added.
The number of insolvent firms reached 23,405 by the end of December, up 11 percent from November. These firms employ 612,000 of the 2.053 million people in employment in December.
Their unpaid liabilities in December dropped 2.5 percent from November to 5.049 billion dinars ($924 million).
"It is obvious that big industries have improved their liquidity," Milisavljevic said. "But it is also evident that a large number of small firms became insolvent."

Another analyst, who asked not to be named, said this proves that big industries, most of them usually managed by government ministers, enjoyed privileges. "The government somehow provides money for them or secures bank lending at a special interest rate," he said.
The number of permanently insolvent firms in 1996 stood at 22,270 with about 550,000 employees and 4.773 billion dinars of unpaid liabilities.
A proposal has been made to place 19,762 firms under receivership with an overall outstanding debt of 4.354 billion dinars but the procedure has been instituted with only 1,450.

"This proves the institution of receivership is inefficient as the government has to make decision to get rid of big loss-making, uncompetitive firms employing most of the workers," Milisavljevic said.
"Eliminating insolvencies would help release funds for investment in healthy companies and pave the way for faster recovery," he added.
